strengths: Clear and practical contribution: a training-free, post-hoc Bayesian treatment (Kronecker-factored GGN Laplace approximation) of the last projection layers of CLIP/SigLIP, which is attractive for large-scale VLMs where retraining is impractical.

The analytic (sampling-free) first- and second-moment approximations of the cosine similarity distribution under Gaussian embeddings is a useful technical device, broadly applicable to any VLM with probabilistic embeddings, and is empirically validated against KDE/Monte Carlo (Fig. 3).

Comprehensive evaluation: zero-shot calibration (ACC/NLPD/ECE) on five standard benchmarks with two backbone families (OpenCLIP ViT-B-32, SigLIP-B-16), plus Bayesian active learning (BALD/EPIG) in cross-domain settings, with paired t-tests used for statistical significance.

Baselines are appropriate and include the strongest relevant competitors (temperature scaling, ProbVLM-style adapter PCME++), and the paper shows the cosine-similarity approximation even improves PCME++'s calibration, demonstrating modularity.

Thorough supplementary material: full derivations of Jacobians and likelihood Hessians for both InfoNCE and SigLIP losses, online Laplace update rules, targeted k-NN selection details, ablations (k-NN distance metric, pseudo-data count grid), and code release for reproducibility.
Honest limitations section (mismatched proxy data for SigLIP Hessian estimation, restricted model classes) and an interpretable qualitative analysis of how variance tracks input corruption.
weaknesses: The moment approximations for the cosine similarity are heuristic rather than rigorous: E[S_COS] is obtained by dividing E[gᵀh] by E[‖g‖]E[‖h‖] and then bounding E[‖x‖] via a triangle inequality, and the covariance is assumed diagonal although Eq. (9) yields a full (rank-limited Kronecker) covariance; the impact of these approximations is not systematically quantified.

Novelty is moderate: Laplace/GGN over last layers is well-established (Laplace Redux, KFAC, etc.); the main new element is the cosine-similarity moment propagation, and the overall contribution is largely a careful integration of known tools into the VLM setting.

Absolute gains are modest: on SigLIP, BayesVLM's NLPD/ECE improvements over vanilla SigLIP are small and it is actually worse in ECE on Flowers-102 and Food-101; improvements over temperature-scaled CLIP in NLPD are also limited, and accuracy is essentially unchanged by design.

The Bayesian framing has foundational gaps: treating the contrastive pre-training optimum as a MAP estimate ignores the normalization/temperature structure, the Hessian is estimated on only a ~30k–327k random subset of LAION-400M (a proxy, mismatched for SigLIP), and the resulting posterior quality for such a heuristic likelihood is not deeply analyzed.

The active learning setup is transductive (the unlabeled test set itself is the query set used for targeting and EPIG), which limits applicability to the more common inductive pool-based setting and somewhat inflates the apparent benefit of 'targeted' selection.

Hyperparameters (pseudo-data count τ, EPIG's γ and β) are tuned on a held-out labeled proxy (ImageNet subset) using test-set-like NLPD, which may not be available in true few-shot/target-task scenarios; sensitivity to these choices is only partially shown.
Coverage of VLMs is narrow (two contrastively pre-trained models); no results for larger CLIP variants in zero-shot calibration, and the approach does not yet extend to generative VLMs.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and practically important problem: cheap, training-free uncertainty quantification for pre-trained VLMs (CLIP/SigLIP), which is timely for safety-aware downstream use.

The methodology is clearly organized and the derivations (Kronecker-factored GGN Laplace over projection layers, Jacobians and likelihood Hessians for InfoNCE and SigLIP in App. B) are provided in reasonable detail, which supports reproducibility.

An analytical, sampling-free approximation to the distribution over cosine similarities is a nice engineering contribution, and it is also shown to improve a probabilistic-embedding baseline (PCME++), demonstrating some versatility.
The paper is candid about limitations (mismatched Hessian data for SigLIP, restricted model families, requirement of pre-training data access), and code availability is stated.
Experiments cover multiple benchmarks and a qualitative corruption study that intuitively illustrates the behavior of the variance estimates.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core machinery is a standard last-layer Kronecker-factored Laplace approximation (Laplace Redux, KFAC-Laplace, online Laplace) applied to CLIP/SigLIP projection matrices. The main new technical piece is the moment approximation of the cosine similarity, which is elementary and built on informal bounding arguments.

The cosine similarity derivation is technically sloppy: Eq. (56)-(57) factorize the expectation of a ratio into a ratio of expectations, ignoring numerator-denominator dependence; the bound on E[||x||] attributed to the triangle inequality is actually a Jensen-type bound; a diagonal covariance assumption is introduced only for this step despite the full matrix-normal posterior in Eq. (9)-(10). The acknowledged variance overestimation in Fig. 3 is a symptom of these approximations.

Evaluation concerns: (i) the temperature-scaling baseline for SigLIP produces implausible results (ECE of 57-65%), suggesting a broken baseline that inflates the relative benefit of BayesVLM; (ii) the pseudo-data count tau and other hyperparameters are selected by minimizing NLPD on an 'ImageNet proxy' that overlaps the evaluation distribution, raising test-set leakage concerns; (iii) zero-shot accuracy gains over CLIP are essentially zero, so the method's contribution is confined to small NLPD/ECE margins.

The active learning setting is transductive (the query set is the test set itself) with weak baselines (random, entropy, 1-NN). No comparison against established VLM active learning / active fine-tuning methods (e.g., Active prompt learning for VLMs, ActiveFT) that the paper itself cites, making it hard to judge practical value. Reported gains in Fig. 4/9/10 are modest and noisy, and the k-NN metric ablation (App. E.2) shows 'no clear trend'.

The method requires access to pre-training data (30k-327k LAION pairs) to estimate the Hessian, which limits applicability to many deployed/closed VLMs; the acknowledged LAION-SigLIP mismatch demonstrably degrades the method (large tau pushing toward MAP), yet this failure mode is not systematically analyzed.

Statistical rigor is thin: 'significance' is based on paired t-tests over individual test samples (not over independent runs/seeds), and results span only 2 model scales and 5 zero-shot datasets, so generality claims ('consistently outperforms') are stronger than the evidence.

Positioning versus closely related work could be sharper: the relation to ProbVLM/probabilistic adapters is discussed, but the practical trade-offs (compute cost of Hessian estimation, quality vs. temperature scaling, which is dramatically cheaper) are not quantified, e.g., no runtime/memory comparison.

strengths: Principled and practical post-hoc approach: applying a Kronecker-factored Laplace approximation to only the last projection layers of CLIP/SigLIP is a sensible and efficient way to obtain uncertainty estimates without retraining, making it applicable to large pre-trained VLMs.

The analytic propagation of uncertainty to the cosine similarity (first two moments) is a clean contribution that is useful beyond this paper (e.g., the authors also show it improves calibration of PCME++), and is validated qualitatively against KDE/Monte Carlo (Fig. 3).

Evaluation covers two model families (OpenCLIP ViT-B-32, SigLIP-B-16), five zero-shot benchmarks, and cross-domain active learning on OfficeHome and ImageNet variants, with significance testing, ablations (k-NN metric, pseudo-data count grid search), and released code.
Results are honest about limitations: the SigLIP/LAION mismatch and its degenerating effect are discussed openly, and the temperature-scaling behavior on SigLIP is reported as-is.
Well-motivated application of Bayesian active learning acquisition functions (BALD, EPIG) with an online Laplace update scheme and targeted k-NN selection to make the approach scalable to VLMs.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the pipeline (Kronecker-factored Laplace + probit approximation + moment matching) assembles well-known tools; the key derivation for the cosine similarity moments is heuristic — E[1/||x||] is replaced by a triangle-inequality bound and the expectation of the ratio is treated as a ratio of expectations, so the 'analytical expression' is an approximation whose error is only empirically (not theoretically) characterized, and it overestimates variance at high similarity.

Gains in accuracy are essentially nil and calibration improvements over simple temperature scaling are modest and inconsistent (e.g., ECE on Flowers-102 and Food-101 for SigLIP is worse than vanilla SigLIP), which weakens the headline claim of 'improved and well-calibrated predictive uncertainties'.

Hyperparameter selection (pseudo-data count τ, temperature for baselines) is tuned on an ImageNet proxy subset, and Hessian estimation uses only 30k LAION samples; for SigLIP the mismatch between Hessian data and pre-training data is acknowledged as degenerative, raising questions about the robustness and practical applicability when pre-training data is closed-source (most frontier VLMs).

The active learning setting uses the test distribution as the query set (transductive), and gains over 'random targeted' selection are visible but not always large or clearly separated in Fig. 4; the statistical treatment (paired t-test over the test set) is somewhat unusual for AL curves.

Baseline coverage is incomplete for the VLM uncertainty literature: no comparison against ProbVLM [68] calibration numbers, deep ensembles/MC-dropout variants on the projection layers, or prompt-based calibration methods [67], making it hard to judge whether the post-hoc Laplace approach is truly the best trade-off.
Claims about 'few-shot classification' applicability are only indirectly supported via active fine-tuning; direct few-shot results are missing from the main evaluation.

strengths: Principled and practical contribution: applying the Laplace approximation post-hoc to CLIP/SigLIP projection layers is a natural but previously overlooked combination, and it satisfies all four stated desiderata (model-agnostic, post-hoc, efficient, training-free).

The ProbCosine derivation is a useful technical contribution: an analytical (sampling-free) approximation to the distribution of cosine similarities between Gaussian embeddings, applicable beyond the authors' own model (demonstrated on ProLIP and PCME++).

Comprehensive evaluation: three model scales (ViT-B-32, ViT-L-14, SigLIP-B-16) across seven zero-shot benchmarks, plus a non-trivial active learning application (BALD/EPIG with online Laplace updates and k-NN targeting), with statistical significance testing (paired t-test).
Strong efficiency story: <5% runtime overhead and essentially unchanged GFLOPs vs. an ~80x cost for TTA, clearly supporting the 'efficient inference' claim.

Good ablations: Hessian trace stability w.r.t. number of data points, k-NN distance metric comparison, qualitative corruption experiments showing mean/variance of similarity behave sensibly under distribution shift, and KDE-based approximation quality checks.
Reproducibility: detailed derivations, hyperparameter settings, and released code.
weaknesses: Hyperparameter selection raises leakage concerns: τ is tuned by minimizing NLPD on an ImageNet subset and temperature scaling is tuned on the ImageNet validation split, while results are reported on benchmarks (CIFAR, Flowers, Food, etc.) that overlap semantically with ImageNet pre-training data. This weakens the validity of the zero-shot comparison and should be discussed more carefully.

Accuracy gains are essentially nil (often slightly negative, e.g., UCF101 in Table 2), so the benefit is purely calibration; on CLIP-large, temperature scaling still beats BayesVLM on several ECE/NLPD entries (e.g., ImageNet-R, SUN397), which makes the advantage over a trivially cheap baseline less decisive.

The ProbCosine approximation is somewhat ad hoc: E[||x||] is bounded via a Jensen/triangle-inequality style bound, normality of embedding distributions is assumed, and the Gaussian approximation of the cosine similarity is validated only qualitatively (KDE plots) rather than quantitatively (e.g., KL divergence, calibration of the variance).

The SigLIP results reveal a practical weakness: with mismatched Hessian-estimation data, the pseudo-data count τ collapses the posterior to the MAP, and BayesVLM degrades on several datasets. Since most popular VLMs have closed-source training data, this limits generality of the claimed desiderata satisfaction.

Missing standard uncertainty baselines and metrics for epistemic uncertainty: no comparison to MC dropout, deep ensembles, or ProbVLM-style adapters, and no OOD detection / selective prediction metrics (AUROC, risk-coverage), which are the usual tests for whether epistemic uncertainty (vs. mere logit rescaling) is genuinely captured.

Active learning evaluation is somewhat limited: OfficeHome with only three domains combined, plus ImageNet variants; no comparison against prompt-learning-based active learning baselines, and the BALD/EPIG improvements, while consistent, are moderate.

Novelty is incremental from the Bayesian deep learning perspective: last-layer Laplace, KFAC, probit approximation, marginal-likelihood-tuned prior precision, and online Laplace are all established tools; the main novelty is their composition for VLMs and the cosine-similarity moment propagation.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and well-organized, with a clean desiderata framing (model-agnostic, post-hoc, efficient inference, training-free) that positions the contribution relative to prior uncertainty quantification approaches for VLMs.

The method is practical and cheap: applying a KFAC Laplace approximation only to the projection layers with an analytic cosine-similarity distribution avoids sampling and adds <5% inference overhead, which is empirically demonstrated (Tables 7-8).

The experimental coverage is broad: multiple backbone scales (ViT-B-32, ViT-L-14, CLIP-huge, SigLIP-B-16), seven zero-shot benchmarks, active learning on OfficeHome and ImageNet variants, and application of ProbCosine to other probabilistic VLMs (ProLIP, PCME++).

The supplementary material contains detailed derivations, ablations (Hessian data requirements, k-NN metric, approximation quality via KDE), and the code is stated to be released, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The core components (last-layer Laplace approximation, KFAC/GGN, probit approximation, BALD/EPIG acquisition) are all standard; the main new piece is ProbCosine, whose derivation is heuristic rather than principled.

The ProbCosine derivation is loose and potentially flawed: Eq. (52)-(53) in App. C.2 replaces the expectation of a ratio E[g·h/(||g|| ||h||)] with a ratio of expectations E[g·h]/(E||g|| E||h||), which is generally incorrect; the E[||x||] bound via the 'triangle inequality' is in fact a Jensen bound, and the resulting moment approximations are not rigorously justified. Approximation quality is only assessed qualitatively on synthetic shifted Gaussians (Fig. 9), not on realistic VLM embeddings.

The claim that 'Bayesian methods have not been employed for uncertainty quantification in VLMs' is overstated; last-layer Bayesian/ensemble methods for CLIP-style models and post-hoc calibration literature are closely related and not adequately compared.

Missing key baselines: ProbVLM [58] and the Dirichlet meta-model [53] are dismissed in Table 1 but never empirically compared, despite being the closest prior work. Cheap alternatives such as MC dropout or deep ensembles over the projection layer are also absent. Without these, the improvement claims are not fully supported.

Results are mixed and sometimes negative: on SigLIP (Table 9), BayesVLM degrades ECE/NLPD on most datasets relative to the vanilla model, which the authors attribute to a data mismatch but do not resolve. Gains over temperature scaling on CLIP are modest, and accuracy is essentially unchanged, so the practical benefit is calibration-only.

In the active learning experiments, a large share of the improvement appears to come from the k-NN targeted-selection heuristic rather than the Bayesian uncertainties themselves; the figures are hard to read and gains over 'entropy (targeted)' are inconsistent across domains.

The Hessian is estimated from only ~327k LAION samples (10 mini-batches) and validity is argued solely via the stability of the Hessian trace, which is a weak proxy for covariance quality; no validation of the full posterior covariance is provided.

Hyperparameter selection (tau, lambda, temperature scaling) relies on an ImageNet proxy tuned by NLPD, which raises concerns about fair tuning across methods and generalization to the reported benchmarks.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and under-explored problem: uncertainty quantification for pre-trained VLMs in a truly post-hoc, training-free manner. The formulation clearly satisfies practical desiderata (model-agnostic, post-hoc, low inference overhead, no additional trained components), and the reported runtime/GFLOP analysis (Tables 7-8) convincingly supports the efficiency claim, especially compared to TTA (~80x cost).

The technical core is reasonably well-developed: a KFAC Laplace approximation over the projection layers combined with an analytic moment-based approximation (ProbCosine) of the cosine similarity distribution, propagated to predictions via a probit approximation. Full derivations for both InfoNCE and SigLIP likelihoods, Jacobians, and likelihood Hessians are provided in the appendix.

The empirical evaluation is broad and careful: three model scales (ViT-B-32, L-14, huge), SigLIP, plus applicability to pre-trained probabilistic VLMs (ProLIP, PCME++); seven zero-shot classification benchmarks; ACC/NLPD/ECE with paired significance testing; and a second, quite different use case (active few-shot learning with BALD/EPIG and targeted k-NN selection).

Several useful ablations are included: sensitivity of the Hessian estimate to the number of data points, grid search over the pseudo-data count τ, k-NN distance metric ablation, runtime overhead, and qualitative approximation-quality checks against KDE of sampled cosine similarities. The limitations section is candid (Hessian estimation requires training data, Gaussian assumptions, projection-layer-only posterior).
Code availability supports reproducibility, and hyperparameter selection uses proxy data (ImageNet val subset, LAION) rather than the evaluation sets, which is good practice.
weaknesses: The main theoretical novelty is limited and partially heuristic. The moment expressions for cosine similarity (Eqs. 7-8) rely on the decomposition E[SCOS] ≈ E[g^T h]/(E||g||E||h||), which is not a valid identity, and the stated justification via the triangle inequality for E[||x||] is incorrect (the correct tool would be Jensen/Cauchy-Schwarz). The Gaussian approximation of a quantity bounded in [-1,1] is also crude; validation of the approximation is only qualitative (Fig. 9). The method is therefore closer to a heuristic moment propagation than a principled derivation, which weakens the 'principled' framing.

Overall novelty is moderate: Laplace/KFAC over last layers with probit averaging is well-established (Laplace Redux, Scalable LA, etc.). The genuinely new pieces are (i) applying it to VLM projection layers with contrastive likelihoods and (ii) ProbCosine. The claim that Bayesian methods 'have not been employed' for VLM uncertainty ignores probabilistic-embedding approaches (ProbVLM, PCME++), which are dismissed mainly because they require training.

Improvements on accuracy are marginal (often within noise, e.g., Table 2) and the substantive gains are in NLPD/ECE, while temperature scaling already achieves comparable NLPD on several datasets. On SigLIP the method is notably mixed, and the paper attributes this to a train/Hessian data mismatch—suggesting fragility in closed-source-data settings, which is admitted as a limitation.

Baseline coverage for the uncertainty-quantification experiments is thin: only vanilla CLIP/SigLIP, temperature scaling, and one TTA method. Missing comparisons include deep ensembles over linear probes, Dirichlet post-hoc calibration, ProbVLM-style adapters, and prompt-tuning-based calibration (C-TPT), making it hard to judge how much the Bayesian machinery adds beyond a well-tuned post-hoc rescaling.

The active learning results are presented only as curves in figures without numeric tables or significance analysis, and in some settings (e.g., certain OfficeHome domains, SigLIP) targeted entropy or random-targeted baselines are competitive; the dependence of gains on the k-NN targeting component (a non-Bayesian contribution) is not fully disentangled.

Several design choices appear tuned for the evaluation rather than principled: τ chosen by grid search minimizing NLPD on an ImageNet proxy, per-τ prior-precision optimization, and EPIG hyperparameters (γ, β) grid-searched on domain-specific validation sets—these add fragility and reduce the appeal of a supposedly hyperparameter-light post-hoc method.
